summary:
East Java stands under the national framework of Indonesia, which is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, this provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. East Java has no provincial carve-out from this framework.

Indonesian law provides no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection based on sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex couples have no recognised legal relationship of any kind. A trans visitor whose foreign documents carry a changed gender marker is dealing with a jurisdiction in which legal gender change requires sex-reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, which indicates the standard Indonesian authorities apply to legal recognition of gender.

Violence risk is elevated by official framing and by mob action. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled. The Diplomat reported in August 2026 that Indonesia's transgender community faces growing repression, with vigilante mobs attacking trans people as the government takes steps to codify anti-LGBT provisions.

Enforcement also takes the form of venue raids. On 22 June 2025, Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

There is a directly documented death of a trans traveller in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in 2022; during a call he was permitted to make, his mother was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody. His mother alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

The only province-level enforcement signal documented for East Java concerns detention conditions rather than prosecution. In February 2025 a transgender content creator became the first transgender detainee held in the province's women's prison after her file was declared complete on suspected defamation.
tangentialFactors:
Sub-national divergence exists elsewhere in Indonesia but not in East Java. Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025; those punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors.

The national courts have not moved toward wider criminalisation. On 14 December 2017 the Constitutional Court rejected, by 5-4, a petition to criminalise gay sex. At the international level, Indonesia voted against the United Nations Human Rights Council resolution establishing an independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2016, 2022 and 2025.

Public attitudes constrain the practical availability of protection. A 2025 Pew survey found that 93% of Indonesians call homosexuality morally unacceptable. Combined with the absence of any anti-discrimination framework, that figure bears on whether a trans visitor who reports an incident can expect an effective response from police or prosecutors.
localsOnly:
Indonesian law provides no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection based on sexual orientation or gender identity, so residents of East Java have no statutory basis on which to contest discrimination in housing, employment or services.

Legal gender change requires sex-reassignment surgery and the approval of a judge. There is no administrative route to a marker change that avoids surgery and court proceedings.

Same-sex couples have no recognised legal relationship of any kind in Indonesia, which removes inheritance, hospital visitation, next-of-kin and property protections as well as any partner-based route to residence.

East Java civil law did not bar authorities from placing the trans woman Isa Zega in a women's prison facility by identity, and with no anti-discrimination framework to contest it, detention by identity remains a matter of institutional discretion. Her placement, recorded in February 2025, made her the first transgender detainee held in the province's women's prison after her file was declared complete on suspected defamation.
outOfScopeNotes:
The penalty for sex outside marriage is reported inconsistently across sources in the inventory, with one figure of up to two years' imprisonment and another of up to one year. The conflict is unresolved here; a visitor should treat the provision as in force from 2 January 2026 with a custodial sentence attached.

No source in the inventory documents prosecutions, venue raids or violence against trans people within East Java itself beyond the February 2025 detention case. Whether the vigilante pattern reported nationally in August 2026 extends to this province is not sourced either way.

Whether the penal-code provisions in force since 2 January 2026 have been applied to foreign nationals in East Java is not sourced. Selective prosecution at the national level is reported, but no case involving a visitor is documented here.

The general encyclopedic entry for East Java produced no substantive finding on LGBT or trans issues, so the province-level picture rests on a single reported case.
